opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's one of the most exciting resources we have, with some important caveats.

The basic idea is that nature has already run the experiments we can't ethically run ourselves. Among roughly half a million people, some carry loss-of-function variants that disable a gene, and occasionally both copies, so they're effectively human knockouts. With exome and now whole-genome sequencing linked to rich phenotypes like health records, imaging, biomarkers, and longitudinal follow-up, you can ask what actually happens to a person when a given gene is switched off. That's enormously valuable for drug discovery. If people lacking a gene are healthy, or even protected from disease, as with PCSK9 and cholesterol, that's strong evidence that inhibiting that target could be safe and effective.

The limitations matter, though. First, complete knockouts are rare. In an outbred population like the UK, most loss-of-function variants are heterozygous, so you're usually studying partial loss. Cohorts with more consanguinity, like Genes & Health in East London or studies in Pakistan, give you many more homozygous knockouts, and they complement Biobank nicely.

Second, there's a healthy-volunteer bias. Participants skew older, healthier, wealthier, and predominantly of European ancestry. Anyone whose knockout causes severe early-life disease won't show up, so you're seeing the tolerable end of the spectrum. That's still informative, but it isn't the whole story.

Third, annotation is hard. Not every predicted loss-of-function variant actually kills the gene. Some escape nonsense-mediated decay, sit in alternative exons, or are sequencing artifacts. You need careful curation, and ideally functional validation, before calling someone a true knockout.

And finally, statistical power. Even at 500,000 people, many genes have only a handful of carriers, so rare-variant burden tests and replication across biobanks like FinnGen, All of Us, and Million Veteran Program become essential.

So overall I'm very optimistic. It's a powerful hypothesis-generating and target-validation tool, especially combined with other cohorts and with computational methods that help us interpret these variants and link them to phenotypes more precisely. It's just not a substitute for thoughtful study design and follow-up biology.

r003.rationale: It mentions longitudinal follow-up, but does not explain that diseases arising as participants age will expand the range of diseases available for knockout studies.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting resources we have for this, with some important caveats.

The basic idea is that if you sequence enough people, you'll find individuals who carry loss-of-function variants in both copies of a gene, so they're effectively natural knockouts. That gives you something close to what we do in mice, but in humans, with decades of health records attached. UK Biobank, with half a million participants and now whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing, is large enough that for many genes you do find a handful of these people, and for a subset you find enough to say something meaningful about phenotype.

Where I get cautious is on a few fronts. First, the population is largely European ancestry and relatively low in consanguinity, so the number of homozygous knockouts per gene is much smaller than in cohorts from populations with higher rates of related marriages, like some of the Pakistani or Middle Eastern studies. For really rare genes, you might have one or two carriers, and you can't build an argument on that. Second, there's a healthy volunteer effect. People who enrolled were, on average, healthier and wealthier than the general UK population. If a knockout is severe enough to cause early death or disability, those individuals simply aren't in the dataset, so you're biased toward tolerable knockouts. Third, calling a variant loss-of-function computationally is not the same as showing the protein is absent. Splicing can rescue, there can be alternative start sites, so you need functional follow-up.

Where it really shines, in my view, is in the pharmaceutical and target-validation space. If you find people lacking a gene who are perfectly healthy but have, say, lower LDL or protection from a disease, that's a very strong signal that inhibiting the protein is likely safe and potentially beneficial. PCSK9 was the model for this, and Biobank lets you run that logic across the genome. Combined with the imaging, the longitudinal linkage to hospital and death records, and the metabolomics and proteomics layers, you can characterize the consequences of a knockout far more deeply than any single clinical study could.

So my overall assessment is that it's a foundational resource, best used alongside more consanguineous cohorts and with a strong emphasis on experimental validation rather than treating the sequence data as the final word.

r001.rationale: The response discusses UK Biobank’s size and possible disease outcomes, but does not say that cardiovascular disease is prevalent enough to provide sufficient outcome events for knockout studies.

r002.rationale: It mentions PCSK9 as a model, but does not report reproducing results from approximately 27 cardiovascular trials.

r003.rationale: The response notes longitudinal records, but does not say that diseases developing in participants over time will expand which diseases can be studied.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential is enormous. Naturally occurring loss-of-function variants give us an opportunity to ask what happens when a gene’s activity is reduced or, in some cases, effectively switched off. With a resource like UK Biobank, you can connect those variants to health outcomes and a wide range of measurements, which could help us understand gene function and identify promising therapeutic targets.

The challenge is that complete human knockouts can be very rare, and a predicted loss-of-function variant doesn’t necessarily mean the gene is inactive. So you need careful validation and enough people carrying the relevant variants to draw meaningful conclusions. It’s a powerful starting point, but the genetic evidence needs to be followed up experimentally.

r001.rationale: The response mentions linking variants to health outcomes, but does not say cardiovascular disease is prevalent enough in UK Biobank to provide sufficient outcome events.

r002.rationale: It does not report reproducing results from approximately 27 cardiovascular trials.

r003.rationale: It does not say that diseases developing among participants over time will broaden the diseases available for human knockout studies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the potential is enormous. UK Biobank gives us a way to connect naturally occurring genetic variation with a rich picture of people’s health. If someone carries a variant that effectively switches off a gene, we can ask what consequences that has—and whether losing that gene’s function might actually protect against disease. That could help identify targets for new treatments.

The challenge is that true human knockouts are rare, and a variant predicted to disrupt a gene doesn’t necessarily eliminate its function. So the scale of the resource is incredibly valuable, but careful validation is essential. I’d see it as a powerful starting point for discovering biology, with further work needed to establish what those discoveries mean.

r001.rationale: The response calls UK Biobank large and describes its health data, but does not mention cardiovascular disease prevalence or say it provides enough outcome events for knockout studies.

r002.rationale: The response does not report reproducing results from cardiovascular trials or give an approximate count of 27.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that diseases developing among participants over time will expand which diseases can be studied.
